notes.meaning: Elihu pauses for a moment to see if Job has anything to say. When Job remains silent, Elihu continues speaking to address other unwise things Job had said.

Elihu asks Job if he really thinks it is right to claim that his cause is more just than God's. Job had never spoken those exact words, but his bitter complaints sounded as if God was treating him unfairly.

Elihu accuses Job of asking what good it does to live an upright life instead of sinning. Job had struggled with why he suffered while evil people prospered, but he had never completely abandoned God.
Elihu promises to give an answer to Job and to anyone else who shares Job's doubts. He believes he can clear up their confusion about God's justice.

Elihu tells Job to look up at the sky and gaze at the clouds high above. If humans cannot reach or control the clouds, God is even far higher above them. Looking at creation reminds us of how great God is compared to tiny people.
Elihu explains that our sins do not hurt God or take away His majesty. Even if a person sins repeatedly, God's nature and power remain completely unharmed.
In the same way, living a good life gives nothing to God that He needs. God already owns everything in heaven and earth, so our good deeds can never put Him in our debt.
Elihu points out that our bad deeds only hurt other human beings, and our good deeds only help fellow people. Our choices affect the people around us, but they do not add to or take away from God.
Elihu mentions that oppressed people often cry out under the heavy burden of cruel rulers. Yet people often cry out merely because of their physical pain, rather than truly seeking God.
The suffering rarely ask where God their Maker is, even though He can give songs of joy in the darkest times. God is ready to comfort people in deep sorrow, but they often forget to call upon Him.

God gave human beings far more understanding than the beasts and made them wiser than the birds. Because people have this gift of reason, they should turn to their Creator instead of simply groaning like animals.
When oppressed people cry out and God does not answer, it is because of their own pride. They complain loudly about the pride of their abusers, yet they refuse to humble their own hearts before God.
Elihu insists that the Almighty will not listen to empty cries. God does not regard prayers that come from selfish complaining rather than true faith and repentance.
Elihu challenges Job for complaining that he cannot see God or understand His working. Even when God seems silent, Job's case is fully known to Him, and Job must wait with patient trust.

Elihu says that because God has delayed His anger and has not swiftly punished Job's rash talk, Job has grown bolder in his complaints. Just because God is patient does not mean He overlooks foolish words.
Elihu concludes that Job is opening his mouth in vain and piling up words without understanding. In his deep sorrow, Job was speaking unwisely about God's ways.
